title: Matsya brings back the Vedas
word: the ten avatars as a series
hookLine: the Vedas slip from sleeping Brahma, and the fish dives after them
carry: the vedas are heard, and handed on by mouth
tomorrow: the gods need a mountain to churn the sea. who holds it up?

lines: MISSING WHEN YOU REACH FOR IT.
cards: Some things you only notice are missing when you reach for them: a charger, a key, a grandmother's recipe. In the Bhagavata Purana's telling, an age is ending, and Brahma, the creator, drifts into sleep.
The Vedas slip from his mouth. A demon has been waiting for exactly that. He snatches the sacred words and dives with them into the deep.
And the fish goes in after him.

teach.b: The demon's name here is Hayagriva. That name came up this week as the horse-headed Vishnu who teaches Agastya; in this story it belongs to someone else, a thief.
Matsya finds him in the deep, defeats him, and brings the Vedas back, so when Brahma wakes and the world begins again, the sacred words are there. Why would God dive for words?
In Hindu teaching the Vedas are shruti, what was heard.

Many Hindus hold that no person wrote them; sages heard them, and they've been handed on by mouth, teacher to student, ever since. Seeds, sages, and now the Veda: the fish keeps what's needed to begin again.

Now the week, one card at a time. Lalita rose from the gods' fire with a sugarcane bow, and desire was given its place back, inside dharma. Her hymn called her name after name, and saying the name was the prayer.
The Adhyatma Ramayana kept the real Sita safe in the fire: many Ramayanas, and Sita never Ravana's. A row of avatars, one Vishnu coming down. A fingertip fish that turned out to be the Lord.
A boat through the end of an age, with a neighbor's ark beside it. And now the sacred words, carried up out of the deep.

how: In images of Matsya, the Vedas are sometimes shown being returned by the fish, and the story is retold from the Bhagavata Purana as part of the series of Vishnu's descents.

games.q: what does “the ten avatars as a series” mean?
o: Vishnu's descents in a row; the fish saves the Vedas
ten demons who steal the Vedas while Brahma sleeps
ten rivers that carry the Vedas down to the sea

games.q: the week's cards — tap the pairs.

s: the Hayagriva who steals the Vedas is the one who teaches Agastya
same name, different figures: a horse-headed Vishnu, and a thief.
in the Bhagavata, the Vedas slip from Brahma as he sleeps
an age is ending, Brahma sleeps, and the demon is waiting.
he also dives after the thief and brings the Vedas back.

games.q: a classmate asks why Vedic chanting is still taught by ear, teacher to student, when every word is printed. by Matsya's dive?
o: they're shruti, what was heard; handing them on by mouth is how they're kept.
printing is new; they'll switch to apps soon.
it's memory practice; the words themselves don't matter.
games.why: Matsya dove so the Vedas wouldn't be lost when the world began again. they're shruti, what was heard, and they're still handed on by mouth.

practice: If you know a mantra, say it once, softly, the way it was taught to you, mouth to ear. Then close your eyes and hear it again in the voice of whoever taught it.
If you don't pray, let a line come back that someone older once handed you, and stay with it for the sit.

wordCard.voice: The ten avatars as a series: Matsya, the first descent, brings the Vedas back up from the deep.

orig.note: Sanskrit veda: the sacred knowledge Matsya carries back up from the deep.

carryVoice: Keep this: the Vedas are heard, and handed on by mouth, and the fish brought them home. That's the week.

sources.ref: Bhagavata Purana 8.24 (the Vedas slip from sleeping Brahma; the demon Hayagriva; Matsya returns them)
